title: perf-regression-tracking-and-triage-notes
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working playbook for investigating serving runtime performance regressions: how alerts land, what dashboards and metrics to check first, an ordered set of profiling steps to narrow down bottlenecks, and pragmatic bisect/canary comparison guidance to identify the root cause and mitigation path. This doc is intended for on-call engineers and owners of model-serving changes.

High-level goals (TL;DR):
- Triage quickly to determine customer impact (percentage of traffic, affected routes/models, latency vs. throughput).
- Determine whether the regression is systemic (infra/runtime) or specific (model, request shape, tenant).
- Collect reproducible artifacts (profiles, traces, benchmark outputs) to enable a bisect or revert.
- Provide a safe rollback/canary strategy and a list of mitigations to restore SLOs.

Initial alert triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Identify alert signal and scope: which dashboard/monitor triggered? Slack alert channel and alert text. Check last-minute deploys (CI/CD) and infra events.
2) Quantify impact: percent of requests above p95/p99, number of affected tokens/sec, number of tenants failing. Use the Perf Dashboards page.
3) Isolate routes/models: filter by route_id/model_version in dashboards. If only one model or route impacted, treat as model/config issue. If broad, treat as runtime/infra.
4) Check recent deploys and rollouts: look at canary timelines, model rollouts, kernel/runtime upgrades, VM/driver updates. Check GitHub PRs and the deployment timeline in the rollouts dashboard.
5) Escalate/assign owner: if impact > 5% of traffic or SLO breach, assign an owner (usually on-call SRE + runtime engineer). Open a JIRA ticket and tag with incident severity.

Dashboards and metrics to check immediately: (order matters)
- Global p50/p95/p99 latency and token throughput (per-cluster, per-region).
- Queue length and backlog metrics (requests waiting to be scheduled).
- GPU utilization (per-GPU), memory pressure, swap activity, OOM counts.
- Model KV cache hit rate and cache eviction rate.
- Batch sizes and batching delay histograms (are we batching less? more?).
- Scheduler backpressure counters (throttles, dropped requests).
- Disk and network IO spikes on hosts serving KV/cache.
- Recent GC/pause metrics for host processes (if using JVM or managed runtime).

Quick classification heuristics:
- If GPU util spikes while latency increases, look for kernel-level regressions, big model changes, or sequence-length shifts.
- If util drops but queue builds up, check for scheduler regression, host affinity issues, or driver crashes.
- If KV cache hit rate drops and latency increases, consider model or prompt-shape changes causing cache misses.
- If regression correlates with a specific region/hostset, suspect infra (drivers, kernel, instance type) or deployment targeting.

Collecting reproducible artifacts (next 10-30 minutes):
- Capture a short timeline (5-15 minutes) of metrics at high resolution and save charts as PNG/PDF.
- Export trace samples for affected requests (distributed trace span capture). Save raw trace JSONs.
- Collect a GPU profile (nsys/torch.profiler) for 1-2 representative requests or a synthetic batch that reproduces the issue. If production sampling is disabled, reproduce in a staging cluster with the same model binary/config.
- Dump per-process perf counters (perf record) and a flamegraph if CPU is suspect.
- Capture model-specific telemetry: KV cache hot-keys, prefix lengths, tokenization distribution.
- Save benchmark runner outputs (throughput, latency percentiles) run with the same config as prod traffic.
- Note environment metadata: model checksum, runtime release tag, kernel/driver versions, deployment ID.

Profiling and targeted investigation steps: (ordered)
1) Reproduce on a small scale: use the benchmark harness against the exact model binary + runtime tag and the same request mix. Reproducible regressions make bisecting tractable.
2) If reproducible, run an end-to-end profiler (GPU and CPU) to see where time is spent: kernel launch overhead, attention kernel hot paths, memcpy/IO waits, Python GC, or orchestration queues.
3) If tail latency is the issue, collect per-token timing (time per decode step) to find whether token generation stalls or a particular step spikes.
4) Inspect batching behavior: are batch shapes different? Is batching delay increased by scheduling changes?
5) Check quantization/unrolling changes: new optimization passes or kernel selection changes sometimes regress certain sequence-length ranges.
6) Verify third-party library versions (cuDNN, CUDA, NCCL) and driver compatibility - mismatch can produce subtle slowdowns.

Bisect and canary comparison guidance:
- Bisecting changes in runtime:
  * If the suspect window is commits between tag A and tag B, run a binary search by deploying intermediate commits to a controlled canary cluster and run the benchmark harness for 3-5 runs.
  * Use the same seed/workload and compare p50/p95/p99 and average token throughput. Small noise is expected; require consistent direction across multiple runs.
  * Automate bisect runs with bench-bisect job (example: bench-bisect --model X --seq-len 512 --requests 2000 --target-tag=<git-ref>) which uploads results to a temporary results bucket.
- Canary comparisons against baseline:
  * Split traffic 90/10 or lower depending on risk. Compare the two cohorts on latency percentiles and error rates. Ensure sampling is randomized and stratified by tenant if necessary.
  * If canary shows regression, collect the same set of artifacts (profiles/benchmarks) from the canary hosts and baseline hosts.

Statistical significance and noise handling:
- Run N>=3 independent benchmark runs per candidate commit or canary. Compare distributions (not just means). Use the Mann-Whitney U test or bootstrap to assert significance for p95/p99.
- Be aware of environmental noise: tenant traffic mix, small GPU multiplexing, and background cron jobs. When possible, isolate in a dedicated test cluster.

Mitigation and rollback playbook: (fastest-first)
1) Hot rollback: revert the runtime/model rollout if regression is confirmed and impact is severe.
2) Reduce concurrency/batching aggressiveness: lower batch size or increase max latency SLO to sacrifice throughput for latency.
3) Route traffic away from affected region/hostset or switch to a compatible model variant.
4) Patch-forward: apply a targeted fix (configuration change or guardrail) and deploy to canary.
5) If root cause is transient (e.g., driver bug), coordinate with infra to roll drivers back or reboot hosts.

Post-incident: artifacts to attach to the ticket
- PNGs of dashboards pre/post regression window.
- Profiling artifacts: nsys trace, perf flamegraph, pprof outputs.
- Benchmark CSVs with seeds and exact commands used.
- Commit range and PRs suspected, plus bisect logs.
- Short postmortem note: timeline, root cause (if found), mitigation steps, follow-ups (test additions, alert tuning).

Runbook snippets (copy-pasteable):
- Slack alert post template:
  "[INCIDENT] perf-regression: p95 latency for route <route> up from <baseline> to <current>. Impact: ~<percent>% traffic. Owner: @<owner>. Initial triage: checking deploys and dashboards. JIRA: <ticket>."
- Quick benchmark command (example):
  "./bench_runner --model model:v2 --seq-len 512 --requests 2000 --parallel 4 --seed 42 --out results.csv"

Open questions / TODOs:
- Add automated snapshotting of a short nsys GPU trace on the first serious p99 spike to minimize manual collection.
- Add bench-bisect automation into CI so suspicious merges trigger an automated bisect job when a perf alert fires.
- Tighten alert thresholds for KV cache drop detection to reduce time-to-detect cache-related regressions.

Notes and references:
- See perf-regression-triage-playbook.json for older checklist variants.
- Bench harness directory: infra/benchmarks/serving.
- Profiling tips: prefer short, representative workloads at production prefixes rather than synthetic extremes.

If you're the on-call owner and need help, ping @eng-runtime on Slack and add the incident channel to the ticket. Preserve all artifacts in the incident bucket under incidents/{jira-id}/ for postmortem and follow-up work.
